Title: The Puma Years
Author: Laura   Coleman
My Review:
The Puma Years by Laura Coleman is a true memoir in every sense—raw, reflective, and grounded in the real-life complexities of jungle conservation work in Bolivia. It took me about a year to finish it, partly because this isn’t a fast-paced story. Instead, it moves with the rhythm of real life, full of moments that are beautiful, chaotic, tiring, and sometimes hard to follow.

One of the more unique elements of the book is how Coleman steers it away from being just a personal journey. She introduces a wide array of people and animals—each a small but significant part of this larger story. While this offers an authentic, collective narrative, it also means that it's not always easy to keep track of every character. But maybe that’s the point. Much like in real life, not every encounter leaves a lasting impression, and many of our experiences are fleeting.

The strongest parts of the book lie in its emotional honesty and deep connection to the natural world. However, it didn’t quite go beyond being “a good read” for me. It’s thoughtful, occasionally moving, and certainly worth reading, but it lacked the kind of resonance or insight that would have made it unforgettable.
